subproblems.title: Squared columns of a derivative are bounded by its squared rows
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ) (f : Euclid n → Euclid k) (v : Euclid n), ∑ i : Fin n, ‖fderiv ℝ f v (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ))‖ ^ 2 ≤ ∑ j : Fin k, ‖fderiv ℝ (fun v => EuclideanSpace.proj j (f v)) v‖ ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Step 3.1, the comparison t(v) ≤ s(v) of the two Hilbert–Schmidt expressions for Df(v), where t(v) = Σ_i|Df(v)e_i|² and s(v) = Σ_j‖Dfʲ(v)‖². It is stated here for an arbitrary map f; no Lipschitz hypothesis is needed. Notation is as in the statement. |·| is the Euclidean norm on Euclid m = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m), and u_i is the i-th coordinate of u ∈ Euclid m.
1. Squared norm in coordinates. For every m ∈ ℕ and u ∈ Euclid m, |u|² = Σ_{i∈Fin m} u_i². Indeed |u| = √(Σ_i |u_i|²) (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq). The radicand is ≥ 0 and |u_i|² = u_i², so squaring gives the claim (Real.sq_sqrt).
2. Squared norm of a functional. For every continuous linear ψ : Euclid n → ℝ, ‖ψ‖² = Σ_{i∈Fin n} ψ(e_i)². Let u := (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (Euclid n)).symm ψ be the Riesz representative of ψ.
 - ⟨u, x⟩ = ψ(x) for every x (InnerProductSpace.toDual_symm_apply).
 - |u| = ‖ψ‖, because toDual is a linear isometry equivalence.
 - The i-th coordinate is u_i = ⟨u, e_i⟩ = ψ(e_i), since EuclideanSpace.inner_single_right gives ⟨u, single i 1⟩ = 1·u_i.
 By step 1, ‖ψ‖² = |u|² = Σ_i u_i² = Σ_i ψ(e_i)².
3. Case 1: f is not differentiable at v. Then Df(v) = 0 (fderiv_zero_of_not_differentiableAt), so each term |Df(v)e_i|² = |0|² = 0 and the left side is 0. The right side is a finite sum of squares, hence ≥ 0. So the inequality holds.
4. Case 2: f is differentiable at v; put L := Df(v). For each j ∈ Fin k, proj_j := EuclideanSpace.proj j is continuous linear, so it has derivative proj_j at every point. By the chain rule, fʲ = proj_j ∘ f is differentiable at v with Dfʲ(v) = proj_j ∘ L.
 - In Lean: HasFDerivAt.comp applied to (EuclideanSpace.proj j : Euclid k →L[ℝ] ℝ).hasFDerivAt and hf.hasFDerivAt, then HasFDerivAt.fderiv.
 - The type ascription fixes the scalar field ℝ, because EuclideanSpace.proj is declared as a StrongDual.
 Consequently Dfʲ(v)(e_i) = (L e_i)_j for all i ∈ Fin n and j ∈ Fin k.
5. By step 2 with ψ = Dfʲ(v), and by step 4, ‖Dfʲ(v)‖² = Σ_{i∈Fin n} ((L e_i)_j)². Sum over j ∈ Fin k and exchange the two finite sums (Finset.sum_comm):
 Σ_j ‖Dfʲ(v)‖² = Σ_i Σ_j ((L e_i)_j)² = Σ_i |L e_i|²,
 the last equality by step 1 with u = L e_i ∈ Euclid k. So in Case 2 the two sides are equal, and in particular the inequality holds.
6. Steps 3 and 5 cover all cases, so Σ_{i∈Fin n} |Df(v)e_i|² ≤ Σ_{j∈Fin k} ‖Dfʲ(v)‖² for every f and v. ∎
proof_key_steps: Squared norms in Euclid m are sums of squared coordinates.
Via the Riesz representative, ‖ψ‖² = Σ_i ψ(e_i)² for every functional ψ on Euclid n.
If f is not differentiable at v, then Df(v) = 0, so the left side is 0 ≤ right side.
If f is differentiable at v, the chain rule gives Dfʲ(v) = proj_j ∘ Df(v).
Exchanging the finite sums gives Σ_j‖Dfʲ(v)‖² = Σ_iΣ_j((Df(v)e_i)_j)² = Σ_i|Df(v)e_i|².

subproblems.title: Exceptional parameter set for the multiplicity-one graph measure
subproblems.statement:
Setting:
- n, k ∈ ℕ; U ⊆ ℝ^{n+k} any set, and W ⊆ ℝ^{n+k} any set with W ⊆ U.
- R = (M, θ, ξ_R) is an integer multiplicity triple in U (Lean IMRep U n), with M = R.carrier (Borel) and θ = R.mult : ℝ^{n+k} → ℕ.
- μ := R.measure = (Hⁿ⌞M) with density θ, where Hⁿ = μHE[n].
- ξ ∈ ℝ^{n+k} and r > 0 with closedBall ξ r ⊆ W, and a ∈ ℝ.
- ι : ℝⁿ → ℝ^{n+k} and ι' : ℝᵏ → ℝ^{n+k} are linear isometries.
- P : ℝ^{n+k} → ℝⁿ is continuous linear with P(ιv) = v and P(ι'w) = 0 for all v, w.
- f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵏ satisfies |f(v) − f(w)| ≤ |v − w| and |f(v)| ≤ r/4 for all v, w.
- Φ(v) := ξ + ιv + ι'f(v), and D := ball (0 : ℝⁿ) (r/2), the open ball.
Assume:
(H1) for μ-a.e. x, x ∈ closedBall ξ r implies θ(x) = 1;
(H2) Hⁿ((spt μ ∩ W) ∖ M) = 0;
(H3) Hⁿ((range Φ ∖ spt μ) ∩ closedBall ξ r) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a, where spt μ = R.measure.support.
Then μ(Φ(D)) ≠ ∞. Moreover there is a measurable set Z ⊆ ℝⁿ such that Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a and, for every measurable h : ℝ^{n+k} → [0, ∞], ∫⁻_{Φ(D)} h dμ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D ∖ Z)} h dHⁿ.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ) (U W : Set (Euclid (n + k))) (R : IMRep U n) (ξ : Euclid (n + k)) (r a : ℝ) (ι : Euclid n →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + k)) (ι' : Euclid k →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + k)) (P : Euclid (n + k) →L[ℝ] Euclid n) (f : Euclid n → Euclid k), W ⊆ U → 0 < r → closedBall ξ r ⊆ W → (∀ v, P (ι v) = v) → (∀ w, P (ι' w) = 0) → (∀ v w, ‖f v - f w‖ ≤ ‖v - w‖) → (∀ v, ‖f v‖ ≤ r / 4) → (∀ᵐ x ∂R.measure, x ∈ closedBall ξ r → R.mult x = 1) → μHE[n] ((R.measure.support ∩ W) \ R.carrier) = 0 → μHE[n] ((range (fun v => ξ + ι v + ι' (f v)) \ R.measure.support) ∩ closedBall ξ r) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a → R.measure ((fun v => ξ + ι v + ι' (f v)) '' ball (0 : Euclid n) (r / 2)) ≠ ∞ ∧ ∃ Z : Set (Euclid n), MeasurableSet Z ∧ μHE[n] ((fun v => ξ + ι v + ι' (f v)) '' Z) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a ∧ ∀ h : Euclid (n + k) → ℝ≥0∞, Measurable h → ∫⁻ x in (fun v => ξ + ι v + ι' (f v)) '' ball (0 : Euclid n) (r / 2), h x ∂R.measure = ∫⁻ x in (fun v => ξ + ι v + ι' (f v)) '' (ball (0 : Euclid n) (r / 2) \ Z), h x ∂μHE[n]
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Steps 0.1–0.5, 1 and 2. This keeps the Hⁿ-measure parts of Steps 1.1–1.3 (the bound on Hⁿ(Φ(Z))) and the identity of Step 2. The passage from Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) to Lⁿ(Z) via the graph area formula stays in the parent.
Notation:
- M := R.carrier; θ := R.mult (ℕ-valued), also read as the [0, ∞]-valued density x ↦ (θ(x) : [0, ∞]).
- μ := R.measure = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity θ; Hⁿ := μHE[n].
- Φ(v) := ξ + ιv + ι'f(v); D := ball (0 : Euclid n) (r/2); B := closedBall ξ r.
- All integrals are lower Lebesgue integrals.
1. Φ. Since |f(v) − f(w)| ≤ |v − w|, f is 1-Lipschitz, hence continuous. ι and ι' are continuous, so Φ is continuous. For every v, Φ(v) − ξ = ιv + ι'f(v), hence P(Φ(v) − ξ) = P(ιv) + P(ι'f(v)) = v + 0 = v. So Φ is injective. Euclid n is Polish and Φ is continuous and injective, so Φ(A) is Borel for every Borel A ⊆ Euclid n (MeasurableSet.image_of_continuousOn_injOn).
2. Φ(D) ⊆ B. For v ∈ D, |Φ(v) − ξ| = |ιv + ι'f(v)| ≤ |ιv| + |ι'f(v)| = |v| + |f(v)| < r/2 + r/4 ≤ r. This uses that ι, ι' preserve norms and r > 0; orthogonality of ι and ι' is not needed.
3. Formula for μ. For every Borel S, μ(S) = ∫⁻_S θ d(Hⁿ⌞M) = ∫⁻_{S∩M} θ dHⁿ (withDensity_apply, Measure.restrict_restrict). The density x ↦ (θ(x) : [0, ∞]) is measurable: R.mult is measurable (R.measurable_mult), and every map out of ℕ is measurable (measurable_from_nat).
4. First conclusion. B is compact and B ⊆ W ⊆ U. So by step 3 and IMRep.locallyIntegrable_mult, μ(B) = ∫⁻_{M∩B} θ dHⁿ ≠ ∞ (note B ∩ M = M ∩ B). By step 2 and monotonicity, μ(Φ(D)) ≤ μ(B), so μ(Φ(D)) ≠ ∞.
5. The non-unit multiplicity set. Let N := B ∩ {x : θ(x) ≠ 1}, a Borel set (B is closed, θ is measurable). Hypothesis (H1) says μ({x : ¬(x ∈ B → θ(x) = 1)}) = 0 (ae_iff). N is contained in that set, so μ(N) = 0 (measure_mono_null).
6. Hⁿ(N ∩ M) = 0. For x ∈ M, θ(x) ≥ 1: R.mult_pos gives θ(x) > 0, and θ(x) ∈ ℕ. Hence, by step 3 with S = N,
 Hⁿ(N ∩ M) = ∫⁻_{N∩M} 1 dHⁿ ≤ ∫⁻_{N∩M} θ dHⁿ = μ(N) = 0 (setLIntegral_mono).
7. Definition of Z. Let Z := D ∩ Φ⁻¹(Mᶜ ∪ {x : θ(x) ≠ 1}). Z is Borel: D is open, Φ is continuous, M is Borel (R.measurableSet_carrier) and θ is measurable. For v ∈ D: v ∉ Z ⟺ (Φ(v) ∈ M and θ(Φ(v)) = 1).
8. Second conclusion: Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) ≤ ofReal a. Let v ∈ Z and x := Φ(v); then x ∈ B by step 2.
 (i) If x ∈ M, then θ(x) ≠ 1 because v ∈ Z, so x ∈ N ∩ M.
 (ii) If x ∉ M and x ∉ spt μ, then x ∈ (range Φ ∖ spt μ) ∩ B.
 (iii) If x ∉ M and x ∈ spt μ, then x ∈ W (as B ⊆ W), so x ∈ (spt μ ∩ W) ∖ M.
 Thus Φ(Z) ⊆ [(range Φ ∖ spt μ) ∩ B] ∪ [(spt μ ∩ W) ∖ M] ∪ [N ∩ M]. Monotonicity and subadditivity (measure_union_le), together with (H3), (H2) and step 6, give Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) ≤ ofReal a + 0 + 0 = ofReal a.
9. Φ(D ∖ Z) = (Φ(D) ∩ M) ∖ N.
 (⊆) If v ∈ D ∖ Z, then by step 7 Φ(v) ∈ M and θ(Φ(v)) = 1. So Φ(v) ∈ Φ(D) ∩ M and Φ(v) ∉ N.
 (⊇) Let x = Φ(v) with v ∈ D, x ∈ M and x ∉ N. Then x ∈ B (step 2) and x ∉ N, so θ(x) = 1. Hence Φ(v) ∉ Mᶜ ∪ {θ ≠ 1}, i.e. v ∉ Z, and x ∈ Φ(D ∖ Z).
10. Third conclusion. Let h : Euclid (n+k) → [0, ∞] be measurable. Φ(D) is Borel by step 1, so:
 - restriction to Φ(D) commutes with taking the density (restrict_withDensity);
 - (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞Φ(D) = Hⁿ⌞(Φ(D) ∩ M) (Measure.restrict_restrict);
 - integrating against a measure with measurable density multiplies the integrand by the density (lintegral_withDensity_eq_lintegral_mul, θ and h measurable).
 Hence ∫⁻_{Φ(D)} h dμ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D)∩M} θ·h dHⁿ. N is Borel, so split Φ(D) ∩ M into (Φ(D) ∩ M) ∩ N and (Φ(D) ∩ M) ∖ N (lintegral_inter_add_sdiff).
 - The first piece lies in N ∩ M, which is Hⁿ-null by step 6, so its integral is 0 (setLIntegral_measure_zero).
 - On the second piece, which is Borel, θ = 1: a point x there lies in Φ(D) ⊆ B and not in N. So θ·h = h there (setLIntegral_congr_fun).
 Therefore ∫⁻_{Φ(D)} h dμ = ∫⁻_{(Φ(D)∩M)∖N} h dHⁿ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D∖Z)} h dHⁿ by step 9.
11. Steps 4, 7, 8 and 10 give all three conclusions: μ(Φ(D)) ≠ ∞; Z is measurable with Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) ≤ ofReal a; and ∫⁻_{Φ(D)} h dμ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D∖Z)} h dHⁿ for every measurable h ≥ 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Φ is continuous and injective with P(Φ(v) − ξ) = v, so it maps Borel sets to Borel sets; Φ(D) ⊆ closedBall ξ r by the triangle inequality.
μ(S) = ∫⁻_{S∩M} θ dHⁿ for Borel S, so μ(closedBall ξ r) < ∞ by locallyIntegrable_mult, hence μ(Φ(D)) ≠ ∞.
N := closedBall ξ r ∩ {θ ≠ 1} has μ(N) = 0 by the multiplicity hypothesis, and Hⁿ(N ∩ M) ≤ μ(N) because θ ≥ 1 on M.
Z := D ∩ Φ⁻¹(Mᶜ ∪ {θ ≠ 1}) is Borel, and Φ(Z) ⊆ off-support part ∪ (spt μ ∩ W) ∖ M ∪ (N ∩ M), so Hⁿ(Φ(Z)) ≤ ofReal a.
Φ(D ∖ Z) = (Φ(D) ∩ M) ∖ N, and ∫⁻_{Φ(D)} h dμ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D)∩M} θh dHⁿ = ∫⁻_{Φ(D∖Z)} h dHⁿ.

subproblems.title: Bounded-function transfer from a two-sided lower-integral comparison
subproblems.statement:
Setting:
- X, Y are measurable spaces with X nonempty (Lean: X Y : Type with MeasurableSpace instances and [Nonempty X]); m is a measure on X and ν a measure on Y.
- D, Z ⊆ X are measurable, S ⊆ Y is an arbitrary set, and φ : Y → X is measurable.
- s : X → ℝ satisfies s(v) ≥ 0 for all v and is integrable on D w.r.t. m.
- a, c ∈ ℝ with a ≥ 0 and c ≥ 0.
Assume m(D) ≠ ∞, ν(S) ≠ ∞ and m(Z) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a. Assume also that for every measurable h : X → [0, ∞] (lower Lebesgue integrals):
- ∫⁻_{D∖Z} h dm ≤ ∫⁻_S h∘φ dν, and
- ∫⁻_S h∘φ dν ≤ ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ENNReal.ofReal(1 + c·s(v))·h(v) dm(v).
Then:
(a) for every measurable g : X → ℝ and G ∈ ℝ with 0 ≤ g ≤ G everywhere, (∫⁻_D ENNReal.ofReal(g) dm) ≤ (∫⁻_S ENNReal.ofReal(g∘φ) dν) + ENNReal.ofReal(G·a);
(b) for every measurable g : X → ℝ and G ∈ ℝ with |g| ≤ G everywhere, |(∫_D g dm) − (∫_S g∘φ dν)| ≤ G·(a + c·∫_D s dm). Here the integrals are Bochner integrals, each computed separately before subtracting.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (X Y : Type) [MeasurableSpace X] [MeasurableSpace Y] [Nonempty X] (m : Measure X) (ν : Measure Y) (D Z : Set X) (S : Set Y) (φ : Y → X) (s : X → ℝ) (a c : ℝ), MeasurableSet D → MeasurableSet Z → Measurable φ → m D ≠ ∞ → ν S ≠ ∞ → m Z ≤ ENNReal.ofReal a → 0 ≤ a → 0 ≤ c → (∀ v, 0 ≤ s v) → IntegrableOn s D m → (∀ h : X → ℝ≥0∞, Measurable h → (∫⁻ v in D \ Z, h v ∂m) ≤ (∫⁻ y in S, h (φ y) ∂ν) ∧ (∫⁻ y in S, h (φ y) ∂ν) ≤ ∫⁻ v in D \ Z, ENNReal.ofReal (1 + c * s v) * h v ∂m) → (∀ (g : X → ℝ) (G : ℝ), Measurable g → (∀ v, 0 ≤ g v) → (∀ v, g v ≤ G) → (∫⁻ v in D, ENNReal.ofReal (g v) ∂m) ≤ (∫⁻ y in S, ENNReal.ofReal (g (φ y)) ∂ν) + ENNReal.ofReal (G * a)) ∧ ∀ (g : X → ℝ) (G : ℝ), Measurable g → (∀ v, |g v| ≤ G) → |(∫ v in D, g v ∂m) - (∫ y in S, g (φ y) ∂ν)| ≤ G * (a + c * (∫ v in D, s v ∂m))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Steps 3.2, 4 and 5, the passage from the two-sided comparison (3a) to clauses (a) and (b), abstracted to arbitrary measure spaces. In the parent: X = ℝⁿ, m = Lⁿ, D = B̆_{r/2}(0), Y = ℝ^{n+k}, ν = μ, S = Φ(D), φ(x) = P(x − ξ), c = 2ⁿ, s = Σ_j‖Dfʲ‖². Conventions: ∫⁻ is the lower Lebesgue integral in [0, ∞] and ∫ the Bochner integral. Fix x₀ ∈ X, which exists because X is nonempty.
1. Preliminaries.
 (i) Z is measurable. So ∫⁻_D F dm = ∫⁻_{D∩Z} F dm + ∫⁻_{D∖Z} F dm for every F : X → [0, ∞] (lintegral_inter_add_sdiff), and ∫_D u dm = ∫_{D∩Z} u dm + ∫_{D∖Z} u dm for every u integrable on D (integral_inter_add_sdiff).
 (ii) m(D ∩ Z) ≤ m(Z) ≤ ofReal a < ∞, so (m(D ∩ Z)).toReal ≤ a because a ≥ 0 (ENNReal.toReal_le_of_le_ofReal).
 (iii) Let u : X → ℝ be measurable with |u| ≤ G everywhere. Then u is integrable on D, being bounded with m(D) < ∞ (Measure.integrableOn_of_bounded). Likewise u∘φ is ν-integrable on S: it is measurable because φ is, it is bounded, and ν(S) < ∞.
2. Proof of (a). Let g be measurable with 0 ≤ g ≤ G; then G ≥ g(x₀) ≥ 0. By 1(i), ∫⁻_D ofReal(g) dm = ∫⁻_{D∩Z} ofReal(g) dm + ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ofReal(g) dm.
 - First term. ofReal(g(v)) ≤ ofReal(G) pointwise, so it is ≤ ∫⁻_{D∩Z} ofReal(G) dm = ofReal(G)·m(D∩Z) ≤ ofReal(G)·ofReal(a) = ofReal(G·a). This uses setLIntegral_const, 1(ii), and ENNReal.ofReal_mul with G ≥ 0.
 - Second term. H := ofReal ∘ g is measurable, so the left comparison hypothesis gives ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ofReal(g) dm ≤ ∫⁻_S ofReal(g(φ(y))) dν(y).
 Adding, ∫⁻_D ofReal(g) dm ≤ ofReal(G·a) + ∫⁻_S ofReal(g∘φ) dν. Commuting the sum gives (a).
3. Key estimate. Let h : X → ℝ be measurable with 0 ≤ h ≤ G everywhere, so G ≥ h(x₀) ≥ 0. Let Δ(h) := (∫_S h∘φ dν) − (∫_D h dm). Claim: −G·a ≤ Δ(h) ≤ G·(c·∫_D s dm).
 3.1 Integrability.
 - By 1(iii), h is integrable on D, hence on D ∖ Z, and h∘φ is integrable on S.
 - s·h is integrable on D ∖ Z (Integrable.mono'). It is a.e.-strongly measurable, since s is integrable on D ⊇ D ∖ Z and h is measurable. Also |s·h| = s·h ≤ G·s, and G·s is integrable on D ∖ Z.
 - Hence (1 + c·s)·h = h + c·(s·h) is integrable on D ∖ Z.
 3.2 Comparison of Bochner integrals. Apply the hypothesis to the measurable H := ofReal ∘ h. Using 1 + c·s ≥ 0 (as c, s ≥ 0) and ENNReal.ofReal_mul:
 ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ofReal(h) dm ≤ ∫⁻_S ofReal(h∘φ) dν ≤ ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ofReal(1 + c s)·ofReal(h) dm = ∫⁻_{D∖Z} ofReal((1 + c s)·h) dm.
 For a nonnegative integrable function u on a set, ∫ u = (∫⁻ ofReal(u)).toReal (integral_eq_lintegral_of_nonneg_ae), and ∫⁻ ofReal(u) < ∞ (hasFiniteIntegral_iff_ofReal). By 3.1 this applies to h on D ∖ Z, to h∘φ on S and to (1 + c s)·h on D ∖ Z. Since toReal is monotone on finite values (ENNReal.toReal_mono),
 ∫_{D∖Z} h dm ≤ ∫_S h∘φ dν ≤ ∫_{D∖Z} (1 + c s)·h dm.
 3.3 Lower bound. By 1(i), ∫_D h = ∫_{D∩Z} h + ∫_{D∖Z} h. Also 0 ≤ ∫_{D∩Z} h since h ≥ 0, and ∫_{D∩Z} h ≤ G·(m(D∩Z)).toReal ≤ G·a. The last bound uses norm_setIntegral_le_of_norm_le_const with m(D∩Z) < ∞, then 1(ii) and G ≥ 0. Thus Δ(h) ≥ ∫_{D∖Z} h − ∫_D h = −∫_{D∩Z} h ≥ −G·a.
 3.4 Upper bound. By linearity (integral_add, integral_const_mul), ∫_{D∖Z} (1 + c s)·h = ∫_{D∖Z} h + c·∫_{D∖Z} s·h. Pointwise s·h ≤ G·s, because s ≥ 0 and h ≤ G. So ∫_{D∖Z} s·h ≤ G·∫_{D∖Z} s ≤ G·∫_D s, the last step because s ≥ 0 and D ∖ Z ⊆ D (setIntegral_mono, setIntegral_mono_set). With c ≥ 0 this gives c·∫_{D∖Z} s·h ≤ G·(c·∫_D s). Hence
 Δ(h) ≤ ∫_{D∖Z} h + G·(c ∫_D s) − ∫_D h = −∫_{D∩Z} h + G·(c ∫_D s) ≤ G·(c ∫_D s).
4. Proof of (b). Let g be measurable with |g| ≤ G everywhere; then G ≥ |g(x₀)| ≥ 0. Let g⁺ := max(g, 0) and g⁻ := max(−g, 0). Both are measurable, 0 ≤ g^± ≤ G, and g = g⁺ − g⁻ pointwise (max_zero_sub_max_neg_zero_eq_self). By 1(iii), g^± are integrable on D and g^±∘φ on S, so linearity (integral_sub) gives
 ∫_D g dm = ∫_D g⁺ dm − ∫_D g⁻ dm and ∫_S g∘φ dν = ∫_S g⁺∘φ dν − ∫_S g⁻∘φ dν.
 Therefore (∫_D g dm) − (∫_S g∘φ dν) = Δ(g⁻) − Δ(g⁺). Step 3 applied to h = g⁺ and h = g⁻ gives −G·a ≤ Δ(g^±) ≤ G·(c ∫_D s). Hence
 −(G·a + G·(c ∫_D s)) ≤ Δ(g⁻) − Δ(g⁺) ≤ G·(c ∫_D s) + G·a,
 that is, |(∫_D g dm) − (∫_S g(φ(y)) dν(y))| ≤ G·a + G·(c·∫_D s dm) = G·(a + c·∫_D s dm). This is (b), with the two integrals computed separately and then subtracted. ∎
proof_key_steps: Split D into D ∩ Z and D ∖ Z (Z measurable), and use m(D ∩ Z) ≤ m(Z) ≤ ofReal a with a ≥ 0.
(a): the D ∩ Z part is ≤ ofReal(G)·m(Z) ≤ ofReal(G·a); the D ∖ Z part is ≤ ∫⁻_S ofReal(g∘φ) dν by the lower comparison.
For measurable 0 ≤ h ≤ G, all relevant integrands are integrable with finite lower integrals, so the comparison passes to Bochner integrals: ∫_{D∖Z} h ≤ ∫_S h∘φ ≤ ∫_{D∖Z}(1 + c s)h.
Hence −G·a ≤ Δ(h) := ∫_S h∘φ − ∫_D h ≤ G·c·∫_D s, using 0 ≤ ∫_{D∩Z} h ≤ G·a and ∫_{D∖Z} s h ≤ G ∫_D s.
(b): write g = g⁺ − g⁻; linearity gives ∫_D g − ∫_S g∘φ = Δ(g⁻) − Δ(g⁺), whose absolute value is ≤ G(a + c ∫_D s).
